/-!
# Erdős Problem 236

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/236](https://www.erdosproblems.com/236)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter Asymptotics

namespace Erdos236

/--
$f(n)$ counts the number of solutions to $n=p+2^k$ for prime $p$ and $k\geq 0$.
-/
def f (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  ((List.range (Nat.log2 n + 1)).filter (fun k => Nat.Prime (n - 2^k))).length

/--
Let $f(n)$ count the number of solutions to $n=p+2^k$ for prime $p$ and $k\geq 0$. Show that $f(n)=o(\log n)$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_236: (fun n => (f n : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun n => Real.log (n : ℝ)) := by
  sorry

end Erdos236

reformulations.difference: The source counts pairs (p,k) satisfying n = p + 2^k, whereas Lean counts exponents in a logarithmically bounded list using primality of truncated natural subtraction.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every representation has 2^k < n and hence k ≤ Nat.log2 n. Conversely, primality of n - 2^k implies that subtraction has not truncated to zero and yields the required prime p. Each exponent determines exactly one p, and the filtered range has no duplicates. In the scratch file, an explicit finite bijection proves, for every n, f n = Nat.card {pk : ℕ × ℕ // pk.1.Prime ∧ n = pk.1 + 2^pk.2}, including n = 0.

review.notes: Both declarations were checked. Lean computations matched f against direct enumeration of solution pairs for every 0 ≤ n ≤ 100. A separate Lean proof establishes that the theorem's little-o expression is equivalent to f(n)/log(n) → 0; log is positive eventually, so its values at 0 and 1 cause no issue. These checks do not use the admitted conjecture. Experiments are in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.
